findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported, so the module fails to compile
findings.body: The new credential update in `getClient` calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. The file's import list only includes jsforce, rrule, zod, lib helpers and the app-store util. This is a TypeScript/runtime error that breaks the whole Salesforce calendar integration, not just token refresh.

findings.title: Computed keys use `z.string().toString()`, so the minimal schema requires a literal "[object Object]" key
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the string "[object Object]", not a pattern matching any key. The minimum schema therefore requires a property literally named "[object Object]" and fails on any real token response. When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, every refresh that goes through this helper (Zoom, Office365, Salesforce) will be rejected with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned".

findings.title: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a SafeParse result, but its return value is stored as the credential key
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns `{ success, data }` (the safeParse wrapper), but this call stores that wrapper as the key: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(...)` followed by `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The credential JSON then becomes `{ success: true, data: {...} }` and the actual access_token/expiry_date fields are no longer at the top level, so the next `googleCredentialSchema.parse` on the stored key will fail. Other callers (Office365, Zoom, Salesforce) correctly use `.data`.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: When the provider's refresh response omits `refresh_token`, this code writes the placeholder string "refresh_token" into the response. Callers persist this as the credential's refresh token, so the next refresh attempt sends a bogus token and fails with invalid_grant, which then marks the credential invalid. The original token should be kept, or the case should be an error.

findings.title: In sync mode it returns a raw fetch `Response`, which callers treat as a parsed token object
findings.body: The sync branch returns the `fetch` Response from the sync endpoint, while the fallback branch returns the provider's native result (e.g. googleapis `res`, a HubSpot TokenResponse, an axios response). Callers read token fields directly: Google reads `res?.data.access_token`, which is undefined on a Response, so it throws. HubSpot sets `expiryDate` from `expiresIn`, which is undefined and yields NaN. Zoho Bigin and Zoho CRM read `tokenInfo.data.error`/`.data.expires_in`, which are not on a Response. The sync endpoint's response is also never checked for `ok`, so an error body would be treated as valid tokens.

findings.title: Outbound sync request carries no authentication and the response is trusted
findings.body: The request to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` as form data, with no shared secret, signature or auth header. Anyone who can reach or impersonate that endpoint can return arbitrary tokens, which are then persisted to the credential. The request also doesn't validate the status or content type before use.

findings.title: Salesforce token refresh now runs unconditionally on every service construction
findings.body: `getClient` now always POSTs to login.salesforce.com and writes the credential, regardless of whether credential sync is enabled. Every Salesforce calendar operation performs a network round-trip and a DB write, and a failed refresh fails the whole service. The `response.statusText !== "OK"` check is also unreliable, since HTTP/2 responses often have an empty statusText, and it should check `response.ok` instead.

findings.title: Malformed payloads cause unhandled exceptions and 500s instead of 400s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError on bad input (line 31), and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throws on wrong key or bad ciphertext or non-JSON plaintext (line 57). Neither is caught, so the request returns a generic 500 and the error may leak. These should be safeParse with a 400 response, and decryption failures should be handled explicitly.

findings.title: Webhook secret is compared with a non-constant-time string comparison
findings.body: The shared secret is checked with `!==`, which leaks timing information. A constant-time comparison such as `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers should be used for a shared-secret check.

findings.title: HubSpot refresh reads `expiresIn` from the sync-mode Response, producing NaN expiry
findings.body: In sync mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a fetch Response, so `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined and `expiryDate` becomes NaN. The stored token's expiry is then corrupted, so the token-validity check behaves incorrectly.

findings.title: Zoho refresh reads `.data` and `.error` from the sync-mode Response object
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a fetch Response in sync mode, so `tokenInfo.data` is undefined and `tokenInfo.data.error` throws a TypeError. Zoho Bigin token refresh therefore fails whenever credential sync is enabled. The same mismatch affects zohocrm/_CalendarService.ts.

findings.title: Zoom expiry becomes NaN when the sync-mode response lacks `expires_in`
findings.body: `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` assumes `expires_in` is present. The sync-mode minimal parse does not guarantee it. If it's undefined, expiry_date is NaN, and `isTokenValid` (`NaN < Date.now()` is false) never reports the token expired, so Zoom tokens are never refreshed again.

findings.title: No tests for the new sync and refresh behaviour despite touching ~20 OAuth refresh paths
findings.body: The PR adds a shared refresh path (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) and a webhook endpoint, and the description admits no tests were added. The bugs above (wrong schema keys, wrapper stored as key, missing import, Response vs token mismatch) would each have been caught by a unit test on these helpers.
